title: Reconstruction benchmark: frontier LLMs recover 3–15% of research ideas from bibliographies alone
subtitle: An anti-leakage protocol across six scientific domains and 643 papers exposes how weak large models still are at the inferential half of scientific reasoning.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: A new benchmark, Reconstruction, posted to arXiv this week and set for ICLR 2026, evaluates whether frontier LLMs can recover a paper's central research idea when given only its pre-publication bibliography. Across 643 papers in six domains and seven frontier models, single-model Match rates land at just 3–15%. A reference-only multi-agent pipeline that layers cross-model review and a Swiss-tournament ranker lifts scores to 23–42% — better, but still far below anything you would call 'reading a bibliography like a researcher.'

The design is what makes the numbers credible. Reconstruction enforces a temporal citation cutoff so the target paper cannot appear in any model's training data, anonymizes reference IDs so cued keywords can't leak the seed idea, and freezes the bibliography per paper so evaluators can't hunt for extra hints. It is a deliberately harder test than 'summarize this abstract' — models have to infer forward from a list of prior work, which is closer to what an early-career researcher actually does when reading a citation trail.

The result lands as several labs — OpenAI's Astra, Anthropic's Claude for Science, DeepMind's discovery loop — are pitching frontier models as scientific collaborators. Reconstruction says the models are already competent at synthesis, but the specific step of naming what a paper's contribution will be from its references alone is still mostly out of reach. Interestingly, the pipeline result also shows structured multi-agent search closes about half the gap, which lines up with a broader 2026 trend: raw model IQ plateaus, and orchestration is where the next 10 points of benchmark performance come from.

For learners and early-career researchers: this is the specific skill your reading practice trains. Sitting with a bibliography and asking 'what is this author about to argue?' before turning the page is not something an LLM will do for you yet, at any tier. If you're using an assistant to speed up literature review, use it for coverage and dedup — and do the inferential step by hand. That is where the paper's value gets made.
